title.en: The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik
title.zh: 阿卡馬利克的夢與皈依

region.en: South Greenland and the bright country above the abyss
region.zh: 南格陵蘭與深淵之上的光明之國

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; event mentioned by Crantz as of the year 1743, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grief for a dead cousin and the lack of a namesake drive Akamalik to kick and awl-pierce his wife — until a new-born babe named for the friend lets him sleep five nights, and then the dream comes: led by a woman over a plain like the ocean's surface, past ball-playing dead men, up three impossible steps, across a fiery abyss to the place so dazzling he had never seen — where the Saviour preaches and leads the song, reproaches his sins, points out tornarsuk in the depths, and bids him seek instruction at Nook. Re-entering his maggot-covered body, he wakes, repents, and is baptised by the Moravian missionaries — a Christian by name, a good man and a loving husband.
summary.zh: 喪友之痛與無名可承，使阿卡馬利克遷怒於妻——踢打錐刺；直到一名嬰兒承了亡友之名，他連睡五夜安枕，夢便來了：一位女子引他越過如海面般的原野，經過擲海象頭球戲的亡者群，躍上三級不可攀的石階，跨過深淵烈火，抵達他從未見過的光明之鄉——救主親自講道領唱，責其罪愆，指出深淵中的托那舒克，並囑他明夏往努克求教。他重入爬滿蛆蟲的軀殼醒來，懺悔前非，受洗於摩拉維亞傳教士——名為基督徒，實為善人與慈夫。

sensitivity.note: Christian-vision syncretism documented as an Inuit-voiced tradition of 1743 (per Crantz); missionary framing retained from the source. Domestic violence recorded as told.

passages.text: In the days when missionaries had come to Nook (Godthaab with New-Herrnhut), but people in other places were still heathens, there lived in the south a clever and skilful seal-hunter named Akamalik, who had a cousin of whom he was very fond. However, it chanced that this friend of his fell ill and died, which caused him much grief and sorely depressed his spirits; as chance would have it, the women of the place at that time brought forth no sons, and his own wife being childless, he could get no namesake for his deceased friend. He henceforth fell into the habit of ill-treating his wife, kicking her and piercing her skin with an awl. After some time it was rumoured that a woman of a neighbouring place had borne a child and named it after his friend; on hearing this Akamalik at once hastened thither, and was so glad at seeing the babe that he was quite unable to sleep for five succeeding nights. Having returned home sleep at length was again restored to him, and then he dreamt as follows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some one peeped in at the window, and calling out for him said that he was to come and get his piece of blubber from a young whale which was just being caught; he at once went out and followed the voice, the owner of which he now perceived was a woman. In running after her he came across a vast plain stretching forth like the surface of the ocean and gradually rising; it became brighter and always brighter — he passed over heaps of sand rolling dreadfully like a mountain-river, and saw a crowd of people playing at ball with a walrus-head. Akamalik would fain have stopped and joined the players, but the woman hurried him on, and almost against his will he constantly followed her; he wondered greatly, for in those people on close view he plainly recognised men who had died a number of years ago. He then came to three high steps which it appeared impossible to ascend; but merely looking at his guide he gave a leap and almost unwillingly mounted them. From the top he again saw before him a great plain and a crowd of people in beautiful clothing — among them he recognised a man in the murder of whom he himself had taken an active part many years ago, and could not but be astonished at hearing people talk in answer to what he was thinking of but had not yet spoken out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Voices were then heard calling the crowd to divine service; the people all sallied forth, and he followed their steps, passing over a dreadful abyss with fires burning down in the depths — then they ascended still higher to a place so dazzlingly bright and beautiful as he never had seen before. Here the Saviour Himself was preaching and leading the song of innumerable people; the Saviour spoke to Akamalik, reproaching him with his sins, at the same time pointing out to him the abyss, where He told him that tornarsuk resided in the depths, and advised him, saying, 'Next summer thou must repair thee to Nook for the purpose of getting instructed.' The Saviour guided him on his way back across the abyss, and thus going downwards on approaching the earth again he (viz., his soul) beheld his own poor body walking backwards and forwards all void of intellect, people believing him to be mad — it appeared very uncouth in his sight, all covered with maggots; but though he greatly abhorred it he nevertheless entered into it, having no other abode.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having thus put on the garb of his body he became like dead and lay in a swoon; by-and-by he recovered his reason and was awake. He then repented his profligate life, went to Nook in the spring, and was baptised by the Moravian missionaries — he not only became a Christian by name, but also a good man and a loving husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A worm fetched from a child's cry at sea and thrown on a barren wife begets Sangiak, who as a small boy strikes two seals with one throw and learns to take the whole flock at a cast. Envious of the double-armed kayaker beloved by all — two harpoons, one in each hand — he picks a quarrel alone at sea and kills him, announces the murder himself, and flees in a kayak his enemies hole at the bottom, stopping the leaks with the stones he fills it with, and returning safe and sound.
summary.zh: 循海上孩啼覓得的蠕蟲擲於不孕之妻身上，遂生桑吉亞克；孩童時代他便一擲雙豹，更練得『一叉收全群』的神技。嫉妒那位雙手各持一叉、受人愛戴的雙叉獵手，他獨自出海尋釁殺之，並親自向其親屬報信；敵人在他的艇底鑿洞追殺，他卻以滿艇石塊堵洞，安然返鄉。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note. Murder recorded as told.

passages.text: A man whose wife could beget no children was advised by an old wise man to set off in his kayak and go out to the open sea, and when he heard a voice like that of a child crying proceed in that direction, and would then find a worm, which he was to take home and throw upon the body of his wife. Having done it the worm disappeared in the body of his wife, who soon gave birth to a son whom they called Sangiak. While he was yet a small child he asked his father for a kayak, and when following his father out to sea surprised him by hitting two seals though he only threw his harpoon once — he acquired the art of always taking the whole flock of seals by only throwing at one of them; at last his father hardly knew how to bring home all the seals he captured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once Sangiak happened to get acquainted with another seal-hunter who could also take two seals at a time, but only by means of two harpoons which he threw one with each hand at once; this double-armed kayaker being much beloved by his companions Sangiak grew envious of him — once when he went out alone with him to sea he picked a quarrel with him and killed him. He then told his father what had happened, and that he would give the relatives of the double-armed notice of the murder; the relatives would fain have avenged it, but he took flight in his kayak, which though his enemies had cut holes in its bottom did not sink — having filled his kayak with stones he stopped the holes with them, and returned to his father safe and sound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 阿特隆瓜克：熊、狼靈與六足獸

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 88 'Atlunguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Despised behind his mother's lamp, fed on what others brought home, Atlunguak bestirs himself only when a deed of special daring which no one else cared to undertake is on hand: he first kills an ice-covered bear, then an amarok, and finally a kilivfak — all fabulous animals.
summary.zh: 被譏為終日蹲在母親油燈後的白食者，阿特隆瓜克唯有在無人敢為的壯舉面前才挺身而出：先殺冰封之熊，再斃狼靈阿馬洛克，終誅六足奇獸奇利夫法克。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note ('only the principal parts selected').

passages.text: Atlunguak was a miserable hunter, despised and mocked by his housemates, who only saw in him a poor wretch always sitting behind his mother's lamp, and feeding upon what the others brought home. But when some deed of special daring which no one else cared to undertake was on hand he at length bestirred himself and braved the danger alone — thus he first killed an ice-covered bear, then an amarok, and finally a kilivfak (all fabulous animals).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 88 'Atlunguak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Nakasungnak: Inside the Ice-Bear, Outside the Gnat-Clouds
title.zh: 納卡孫納克：熊腹之中，蚊雲之下

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Presumptuous among boat-people who have no kayaks, Nakasungnak ignores every warning: he leaps knife-in-hand down the ice-bear's open mouth and comes out between its ribs hairless and shivering; he scorns the advice for catching the birds that can speak and the little fishes with both eyes on one side, and gets none; he stays outside when the gnat-clouds the size of sea-fowls with arrow-point stings roll in like broken clouds from the south — and only a skeleton is found beneath the boat.
summary.zh: 在只有船沒有皮艇的北方人之中狂妄自負的納卡孫納克，無視一切告誡：持刀躍入冰熊張開的大口，從肋間破壁而出，毛髮盡脫、寒戰不止；不聽捕會說話的鳥與雙眼同側小魚的指點，一無所獲；蚊雲如碎雲自南方壓境——群鳥大小、蝟刺如鏃——他獨自留在外面，眾人尋見的只是艇底下一副骸骨。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; death by gnats recorded as told.

passages.text: Nakasungnak travelled far up north, and settled down with some people who used boats, but no kayaks; he was very presumptuous and obstinate. His new place-fellows told him that before long the ice-covered bear would make its appearance, that it was very dangerous, and for mere men a deed impracticable to slay it — but Nakasungnak, nothing heeding, set out to encounter the terrible animal; on discovering it he ran in upon it only armed with a knife, and instantly disappeared down its open mouth. The bear was then seen to totter, and soon after fell down dead; on approaching it they observed a knife sticking out between its ribs — when the hole was widened Nakasungnak jumped out of it, but his hair as well as the skin of his face had come off, and shivering with cold and ague he ran away to the house. In the meantime the bear's flesh served them for food the greater part of the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards they told Nakasungnak how to behave when they were going to catch the birds that could speak, and the little fishes with both eyes on one side; the swarms of birds and fishes appeared — but Nakasungnak would not follow the advice they gave him, and consequently got none. Lastly they told him that gnats were soon expected, the size of sea-fowls, and with stings like the point of an arrow; when the swarms were approaching and seen to come on like broken clouds from the south the people had to retreat to their tents and close them with all care — Nakasungnak however again disregarded their warnings and took no notice of what they had said. When the clouds appeared and all the others sped into their tents he remained outside; when all was over and they went out to look for Nakasungnak they found only a skeleton lying beneath the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak'; not verbatim.

region.en: The brothers' kayaking waters and the rubbish-heap refuge
region.zh: 兄弟們的獵海與垃圾堆中的藏身處

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Reproached into a secret miscarriage, the only sister's child gains intellect and becomes an anghiak: a dog's skull for a kayak, a man's arm-bone for a paddle — nightly at the mother's breasts, daily capsizing her kayaking brothers one after another. Its revenge done, it repents, flees north, frightens a conjuring-house to death, and hides in a rubbish-heap; when the angakok's examination draws out the mother's confession — 'What I brought forth was no real child' — the anghiak feels a pain in its head and dies as she tells her tale.
summary.zh: 在兄弟的斥責下偷偷流產的獨妹，其胎兒竟得神智化為安吉亞克：以犬首為艇、人臂骨為槳——夜夜伏在母親胸前吮乳，日日逐一掀翻獵海中的舅舅們。復仇既畢，它心生悔意，北遁嚇死一座降神屋的人，藏身垃圾堆中；巫師勘問之下，母親終於吐實——『我生的不是真正的孩子』——話音未落，安吉亞克頭痛欲裂，隨她的講述氣絕而亡。

sensitivity.note: Concealed-birth ghost (anghiak) and infanticide recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A company of brothers had a single sister and would not allow her to marry; nevertheless, having many suitors, she finally came to be with child, and because of her brothers' reproaches secretly had a miscarriage — but the child got intellect and became an anghiak. It picked up the skull of a dog using it as a kayak, and the bone of a man's arm for a paddle; every night it used to creep into the house and lie down to suckle its mother's breasts, but during the day-time it was about pursuing her brothers when they were kayaking, and made them capsize and perish one after another. Having accomplished its revenge it repented its deeds and fled to the north, where it slipped down in the doorway of a house in which a conjuration was going on — the angakok (by means of his second-sight) at once observed its approach, and when the people of the house had got a light and went to look for it they were all frightened to death. It then became still more powerful, but went back again to its mother's abode and found a refuge in a heap of rubbish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: It now happened that the angakok of the place was about to perform a conjuration for the purpose of finding out what had caused the brothers' destruction; the sister, on being examined, first denied but finally confessed her sin, saying, 'What I brought forth was no real child' — no sooner had she pronounced these words than the anghiak felt a pain in its head, and while she continued her tale it lost its senses and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak'; not verbatim.

region.en: The moon-man's house above the earth

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Fleeing mankind, Kanak is lifted up in the way of the dead to the moon-man's house — guarded by a terrible dog, entered past a skeleton-backed serving woman, regaled while an old hag licks her own back to tempt him to laugh (the little-finger nail under the knee is the antidote) — until she leaves knife and platter behind, threatening to overthrow the pillars of heaven. Shown the hatch from which the moon-man blows the snow upon the earth, Kanak is pushed down through the opening, guided home by his grandmother's spirit, and grows a celebrated angakok.
summary.zh: 遁世的卡納克被舉上亡者之路，抵達月神之屋——大犬守門、龍骨架背的侍女上菜；一名舔着自己後背、百般逗人發笑的老嫗舞入堂中（以小指指甲擦膝即可忍笑）——她倉皇逃走，留下刀與盤，揚言『不還我便掀翻天柱』。月神自地板的活門向人間吹雪，最後把卡納克推下天梯；祖母的魂魄一路護送他回到地面——他日後成為名震一方的巫師。

sensitivity.note: Moon-man cycle (compare Rink tale 19's Moon Man and the obstinate man, cross-ref inuit-obstinate-man-moon). Fragmentary form per Rink.

passages.text: Kanak, on fleeing from mankind, felt himself lifted up from the ground, and following the way of the dead; at length he lost his senses, and on awakening again found himself in front of the house where the spirit (or owner) of the moon resided. This man of the moon assisted him to get inside, which was a perilous undertaking, the entrance being very large and guarded by a terrible dog; the moon-man having then breathed upon Kanak in order to ease the pain that racked his limbs and having restored him to health spoke thus: 'By the way thou earnest no man ever returned; this is the way thou must take' — upon which he opened a door and pointed out to him a hole in the floor from which he could overlook the surface of the earth with all the dwelling-places of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.

passages.text: He regaled him with eating which was served and brought in by a woman whose back was like that of a skeleton; Kanak was getting afraid on perceiving that, on which the moon-man said, 'Why, that's nothing; but lo! soon the old woman will appear who takes out the entrails of every one she can tempt to laugh. If thou canst not withhold thy smiles thou only needst to rub thy leg underneath the knee with the nail of thy little finger.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon after the old hag entered dancing and whirling about, licking her own back and putting on the most ridiculous gestures; but when Kanak rubbed his leg with the nail of his little finger she gave a sudden start, at which the moon-man seized her and threw her down in the entrance — she went off, but afterwards a voice was heard, 'She has left her knife and her platter, and if she does not get both she says she will overthrow the pillars of heaven.' The moon-man having thrown the knife and platter down the entrance again opened the hatch in the floor, and blowing through a great pipe showed Kanak how he made it snow upon the earth; lastly he said to him, 'Now it is time to leave me, but do not be the least afraid, lest thou never shalt come alive' — he then pushed him down through the opening, on which Kanak swooned; on recovering he heard the voice of his grandmother, whose spirit had followed and taken care of him, and at length reached the earth's surface, arose and went to his home, after which he grew a celebrated angakok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.

title.en: The Barren Wife Taken by the Moon-Man

region.en: Winter night and the moon-man's sledge

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (A Barren Wife), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ill-treated by her husband, a barren wife goes off one winter night and meets the moon-man driving in his sledge, who takes her home with him; many days after, in spring, she appears again and returns to her husband — ere long perceiving she is with child, she gives birth to a son, who when he grows up is taken away by the moon-man.
summary.zh: 被丈夫苛待的不孕婦於某個冬夜離家，遇見駕橇而來的月神，被帶回月宮；次年春天她重返夫家——不久便覺有孕，產下一子；孩子長大後被月神接走。

passages.text: A Barren Wife, who was treated badly by her husband, went off one winter night and met with the moon-man, who came driving in his sledge, and took her along with him to his home. Many days after in spring she again appeared and went to live with her husband; ere long she perceived that she was with child, and gave birth to a son who when he grew up was taken away by the moon-man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (A Barren Wife); not verbatim.

title.en: Manguarak and the Moon-Man: The Wolffish Boast
title.zh: 曼瓜拉克與月神：狼魚之誇

region.en: Winter ice and the moon-sledge ride

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ignoring his father's warnings, Manguarak catches a white whale with a black spot on one side — one of the chase-animals set apart for the spirit of the moon — and is challenged to fight on the ice. The duel becomes a boast-tally of every bird, seal, and whale ever chased; at the halibut-fishing he once helped haul up a keraK (wolffish), at which the moon-man exclaims 'What art thou saying, man?' — as a child he was so terrified at seeing such a fish hauled up that he never dared pursue it. 'Now that I know thou hast caught an animal which I never ventured to pursue, I will do thee no harm... come along with me and see my place' — one dog, a flying sledge, the dark cliff of the entrail-cutting hag.
summary.zh: 不聽父親告誡的曼瓜拉克，獵得側身帶黑斑的白鯨——那是月神專屬的獵物——被月神下戰書到冰面。比武竟成了『生平獵物大清點』；說到捕大比目魚時曾順手拉上一條狼魚，月神失聲——『你說什麼？』——他幼時見人拉起此魚嚇破了膽，從此不敢獵它。『既然你擒住了我從不敢追的野獸，我便不傷你……隨我去看我的居所吧』——單犬駕橇、凌空而馳，途經那割取內臟的老嫗棲身的黑崖。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary moon-myth; the boast-duel inverts the usual combat. Fragmentary form per Rink.

passages.text: Manguarak, unheeding the warnings of his father, caught a white whale which, having a black spot on one side, was known to belong to the animals of chase set apart for the spirit of the moon. On a fine winter night the moon-man was heard to call him outside and challenge him to fight; when he came down upon the ice the moon-man said, 'Well, we will presently begin, but first let us name all the animals of chase we have caught during our lifetime' — they then, each in his turn, named the different sorts of birds, seals, and whales they had chased; and beginning with the fishes Manguarak went on to tell how he once assisted at a halibut-fishing when they happened to haul up a keraK (wolffish).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.

passages.text: On hearing this the moon-man exclaimed, 'What art thou saying, man? Now just wait, and listen to me' — he then went on to tell how, when a child and still living among mankind, he had once seen some people haul up a fish of that same kind, at which he was so terrified that he had never since tried to catch that fish. 'And now that I know thou hast caught an animal which I never ventured to pursue, I will do thee no harm. I begin, in fact, rather to like thee; so come along with me and see my place.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.

passages.text: Manguarak accordingly went up to ask his father's permission, which having gained he returned to the ice, where he found the moon-man waiting with a sledge drawn only by a single dog; when he had taken his place on the sledge away they drove at a great pace, and gradually rising from the ground seemed to fly through the air. At midnight they came to a high land upon which they still travelled on; they went through a valley covered with snow, and had to pass by a dark-looking cliff inside of which lived the old hag who was wont to cut out the entrails of people who could not forbear laughing — as to the rest of the adventures of Manguarak they are much the same as those encountered by Kanak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.
